tool.name: Gradle
tool.tagline: Flexible, incremental build tool for JVM, Android and Kotlin projects
tool.description: Gradle is the build automation tool behind most Java, Kotlin and Android projects. Build scripts written in Kotlin or Groovy declare plugins, dependencies and tasks, and Gradle runs only what changed, with caching and parallelism. Knowing it lets you build, test and publish JVM software and fix the build problems every team hits.

concepts.name: The wrapper and the command line
concepts.summary: Run builds with the Gradle wrapper (gradlew), understand the standard lifecycle tasks and common flags.
concepts.why: Every Gradle project is driven from gradlew; knowing the basic commands is table stakes for JVM and Android work.
concepts.body:
Gradle projects ship a **wrapper**: the scripts `gradlew` (Unix) and `gradlew.bat` plus `gradle/wrapper/gradle-wrapper.properties`, which pins the exact Gradle version. Running `./gradlew` downloads that version on first use, so every developer and CI machine builds with the same Gradle. Always use the wrapper rather than a globally installed `gradle`; update it with `./gradlew wrapper --gradle-version 9.1`.

Common commands:

- `./gradlew build` compiles, runs tests and assembles artifacts.
- `./gradlew test`, `./gradlew run` (with the `application` plugin), `./gradlew clean`.
- `./gradlew tasks` lists available tasks; `./gradlew help --task test` explains one.
- `./gradlew projects` and `./gradlew dependencies` inspect the build.

Useful flags: `-q` quiet, `--info` / `--debug` for more output, `--stacktrace` on failures, `--offline` to use only the local cache, `-x test` to skip a task, `--continue` to run as much as possible after a failure, and `-p dir` to build another directory.

Gradle keeps a **daemon** process running between builds to stay fast; `./gradlew --stop` stops it. Settings for the daemon, parallelism and the JVM live in `gradle.properties`.

Task names can be abbreviated by camel-case initials: `./gradlew cT` runs `compileTestJava` if unambiguous.
concepts.code:
# Pin and fetch the project's Gradle version (committed to git)
cat gradle/wrapper/gradle-wrapper.properties | grep distributionUrl
# distributionUrl=https\://services.gradle.org/distributions/gradle-9.1-bin.zip

./gradlew build                 # compile + test + assemble
./gradlew test --tests "com.acme.*"   # run a subset of tests
./gradlew build -x test         # skip the test task
./gradlew run --args="--port 8080"    # application plugin
./gradlew tasks --all           # every task, including internal ones
./gradlew dependencies --configuration runtimeClasspath
./gradlew clean build --offline --stacktrace
./gradlew wrapper --gradle-version 9.1   # upgrade the wrapper
./gradlew --stop                # stop the background daemon
takeaways: Use ./gradlew, never a global gradle, so versions match everywhere
build = compile + test + assemble; -x skips a task
tasks, dependencies and help --task inspect the build
A daemon keeps builds fast between runs
pitfalls: Committing a project without the wrapper files, so teammates build with different Gradle versions.

options: Builds the project but skips the test task
quiz.explain: -x excludes the named task (and tasks only it depends on) from the run.

concepts.name: Build scripts and settings
concepts.summary: Read a build.gradle.kts and settings.gradle.kts: plugins, repositories, dependencies and the project layout.
concepts.why: The build script is where every configuration change happens; you need to read it fluently.
takeaways: settings.gradle.kts names the build and lists subprojects
build.gradle.kts applies plugins, repositories and dependencies
The java plugin defines the src/main and src/test layout and the build tasks
Toolchains pin the JDK used to compile

quiz.q: Where do you list the subprojects of a multi-project build?
quiz.explain: include(...) in settings.gradle.kts defines the projects of the build.

concepts.name: Declaring dependencies
concepts.summary: Add libraries with implementation, api, compileOnly, runtimeOnly and test configurations, and inspect the resolved graph.
concepts.why: Most build changes are dependency changes; using the right configuration keeps compile classpaths lean and APIs clean.
concepts.body:
Dependencies are declared in the `dependencies { }` block as `"group:name:version"` coordinates, assigned to a **configuration** that says when they are needed:

- `implementation`: needed to compile and run your code, but not exposed to consumers of your library. The default choice.
- `api` (from the `java-library` plugin): part of your public API; consumers get it on their compile classpath too.
- `compileOnly`: available at compile time only (annotations, provided servers). `runtimeOnly`: only at run time (JDBC drivers, logging backends).
- `testImplementation`, `testRuntimeOnly`: the same for tests.
- `annotationProcessor` for tools like Lombok or MapStruct.

Gradle downloads artifacts from the `repositories { }` you list (`mavenCentral()`, `google()`, `mavenLocal()`, or a company Nexus/Artifactory) and caches them in `~/.gradle/caches`.

**Transitive** dependencies come along automatically. When two paths need different versions of the same library, Gradle picks the **highest** version by default (not "nearest" like Maven). See the result with `./gradlew dependencies` or `./gradlew dependencyInsight --dependency jackson-databind`.

Dynamic versions (`1.+`) and `latest.release` make builds non-reproducible; prefer exact versions. Rich versions (`strictly`, `prefer`) and `constraints { }` adjust transitive versions without declaring a direct dependency. Project dependencies use `implementation(project(":lib"))`.
takeaways: implementation hides a dependency from consumers; api exposes it
compileOnly/runtimeOnly split compile and run time
Gradle picks the highest version among conflicting transitive versions
dependencyInsight explains why a version was chosen
pitfalls: Using api for everything, which drags your internals onto every consumer's compile classpath.

quiz.q: A library you build uses Jackson only inside its implementation. Which configuration should you use?
quiz.explain: implementation keeps Jackson off consumers' compile classpath while still compiling and running your code with it.

concepts.name: Running tests
concepts.summary: Configure the test task for JUnit 5, filter tests, see output and reports, and fail fast.
concepts.why: Tests run through Gradle in CI and locally; knowing its knobs saves hours of debugging.
concepts.body:
The `java` plugin adds a `test` task that compiles `src/test/java` and runs the tests. For JUnit 5 (Jupiter), add `testImplementation("org.junit.jupiter:junit-jupiter:...")` plus `testRuntimeOnly("org.junit.platform:junit-platform-launcher")` and tell Gradle to use the JUnit Platform: `tasks.test { useJUnitPlatform() }`. Gradle 8.x+ also offers `testing { suites { ... } }` with `useJUnitJupiter()` to declare this declaratively.

Running and filtering:

- `./gradlew test` runs everything; `--tests "com.acme.UserTest"` or `--tests "*Integration*"` filters by class or method pattern.
- `--rerun-tasks` or `test --rerun` forces a rerun; otherwise Gradle skips tests whose inputs are unchanged (UP-TO-DATE).
- `--fail-fast` stops after the first failure; `--continue` runs other tasks even if tests fail.

Results appear in `build/reports/tests/test/index.html` and XML in `build/test-results/` for CI tools. By default Gradle shows only failures; configure `testLogging { events("passed", "failed"); showStandardStreams = true }` to see output.

Tests run in a separate JVM: set `maxParallelForks` to run classes in parallel, `jvmArgs`, `systemProperty("env", "ci")` and `environment(...)` to configure it. Use tags or separate source sets / test suites (`integrationTest`) to keep slow integration tests out of the fast loop.
takeaways: useJUnitPlatform() enables JUnit 5
--tests filters; --rerun forces re-execution of up-to-date tests
Reports land in build/reports/tests and build/test-results
maxParallelForks and tags speed up the test loop
pitfalls: Wondering why tests 'didn't run': they were UP-TO-DATE because nothing changed.

quiz.q: You run ./gradlew test twice without changes. What happens the second time?
options: The test task is skipped as UP-TO-DATE
quiz.explain: Gradle's incremental build skips tasks whose inputs and outputs are unchanged.

concepts.name: Tasks, dependencies and lifecycle
concepts.summary: Register custom tasks, wire dependsOn, understand configuration vs execution phases and task types like Copy and Exec.
concepts.why: Custom tasks automate everything beyond compilation, and the phases explain most puzzling build behavior.
concepts.body:
A build is a graph of **tasks**. Running `./gradlew build` executes `build` and everything it depends on, in dependency order, each task at most once.

Gradle runs in phases:

1. **Initialization**: settings script, which projects exist.
2. **Configuration**: every build script runs, registering tasks and wiring them. Nothing should do real work here.
3. **Execution**: only the requested tasks (and their dependencies) run their actions.

Register tasks lazily with `tasks.register("name") { }`; the block runs only when the task is needed. Actions go in `doLast { }` / `doFirst { }`; code outside them runs at configuration time on every build, which is a classic performance mistake.

Typed tasks give you ready-made behavior: `Copy`, `Zip`, `Exec`, `Delete`, `JavaExec`, `Sync`. Configure them with `tasks.register<Copy>("stage") { from("docs"); into(layout.buildDirectory.dir("staging")) }`.

Wiring: `dependsOn("other")` forces order and inclusion; `mustRunAfter` orders without requiring; `finalizedBy` runs cleanup afterwards. When one task consumes another's output, prefer passing the output **provider** (`from(tasks.named("jar"))`) so Gradle infers the dependency.

`group` and `description` make a task show up nicely in `./gradlew tasks`. Use `tasks.named("test") { }` to modify an existing task rather than creating a duplicate.
takeaways: Configuration phase runs all scripts; execution runs only requested tasks
Put work in doLast/doFirst, not in the configuration block
Typed tasks (Copy, Exec, Zip) cover common jobs
Wire tasks via outputs/providers so dependencies are inferred
pitfalls: Calling expensive code (shelling out, reading files) directly in a task's configuration block.

quiz.q: Where should the code that actually copies files in a custom task go?
quiz.explain: Actions run in the execution phase; configuration-block code runs on every build whether the task is requested or not.

concepts.name: Plugins and conventions
concepts.summary: Apply core and community plugins with the plugins block, pin versions, and understand what conventions they add.
concepts.why: Plugins are how Gradle supports Kotlin, Android, Spring Boot, code quality and publishing.
concepts.body:
Gradle itself is small; **plugins** add tasks, configurations and conventions. Apply them in the `plugins { }` block, which must be the first block in the script:

```kotlin
plugins {
    java                                        // core plugin, no version
    id("org.springframework.boot") version "3.4.4"
    kotlin("jvm") version "2.1.20"
}
```

Core plugins (`java`, `java-library`, `application`, `maven-publish`, `jacoco`) are bundled. Community plugins are resolved from the **Gradle Plugin Portal** by default, or from repositories listed in `pluginManagement { repositories { } }` in `settings.gradle.kts`. Versions are pinned there or in the version catalog; in a multi-project build, declare a plugin version once (often `apply false` in the root) and apply it without a version in subprojects.

What plugins give you:

- `java-library` adds `api` and ABI-aware compile avoidance.
- `application` adds `run` and `installDist` with start scripts.
- `org.springframework.boot` adds `bootRun` and `bootJar`.
- `com.android.application` turns a project into an Android app.
- `jacoco`, `checkstyle`, `spotless` for coverage and style.

Each plugin has an **extension** for configuration (`java { }`, `application { }`, `springBoot { }`). Prefer `plugins { }` over the legacy `apply(plugin = ...)`, which doesn't support type-safe accessors. You can write your own convention plugins in `buildSrc` or an included build (Advanced).
takeaways: plugins { } must come first; community plugins need a version
Core plugins are bundled; others come from the Plugin Portal or configured repositories
Each plugin adds tasks and an extension block to configure it
Pin plugin versions once per build

quiz.q: Why does id("java") not need a version while id("org.springframework.boot") does?
options: java is a core plugin bundled with Gradle; Boot is resolved from a repository
Versions are optional for all plugins
quiz.explain: Core plugins ship with the Gradle distribution; third-party plugins are downloaded at a specific version.

concepts.name: Version catalogs
concepts.summary: Centralize dependency and plugin versions in gradle/libs.versions.toml and use type-safe libs accessors.
concepts.why: Catalogs keep versions consistent across subprojects and are the modern standard in Android and JVM builds.
concepts.body:
A **version catalog** declares dependency coordinates and versions once, in `gradle/libs.versions.toml`, and every build script references them through the type-safe `libs` accessor.

```toml
[versions]
junit = "5.11.4"
kotlin = "2.1.20"

[libraries]
guava = { module = "com.google.guava:guava", version = "33.4.0-jre" }
junit-jupiter = { module = "org.junit.jupiter:junit-jupiter", version.ref = "junit" }

[bundles]
testing = ["junit-jupiter"]

[plugins]
kotlin-jvm = { id = "org.jetbrains.kotlin.jvm", version.ref = "kotlin" }
```

Then `implementation(libs.guava)`, `testImplementation(libs.bundles.testing)` and `plugins { alias(libs.plugins.kotlin.jvm) }`. Dashes in names become dots in accessors.

Benefits: one place to bump versions, IDE completion, no string typos, and tooling such as Renovate and Dependabot understands the file. `version.ref` shares a version among related artifacts (all Kotlin or all Jackson modules), and **bundles** group libraries that are always used together.

The catalog named `libs` is picked up automatically; additional catalogs can be declared in `dependencyResolutionManagement { versionCatalogs { } }` in `settings.gradle.kts`, or published as a `.toml` artifact for sharing across repositories.

Catalogs don't change resolution rules: they only provide coordinates. Use **platforms/BOMs** (`implementation(platform(libs.spring.bom))`) when you need to align transitive versions.
takeaways: gradle/libs.versions.toml holds versions, libraries, bundles and plugins
Use libs.xxx accessors; dashes become dots
version.ref shares one version across related artifacts
Catalogs provide coordinates; BOMs/platforms align transitive versions

quiz.q: How is a catalog library named junit-jupiter referenced in build.gradle.kts?
quiz.explain: Accessor names replace dashes with dots: libs.junit.jupiter.

concepts.name: Multi-project builds
concepts.summary: Split a build into subprojects, share configuration with convention plugins, and depend on sibling projects.
concepts.why: Real codebases have many modules; structuring them well keeps builds fast and dependencies honest.
concepts.body:
A **multi-project build** has one `settings.gradle.kts` that includes several subprojects, each with its own `build.gradle.kts` in its folder:

```kotlin
rootProject.name = "shop"
include("core", "api", "app")
```

Subprojects are addressed by path: `:core`, `:services:billing` for nested folders. Run a task in one project with `./gradlew :api:test`; running `./gradlew test` from the root runs it in every project that has it.

Projects depend on each other with `implementation(project(":core"))`. Gradle then builds `core` first and uses its jar (with compile avoidance when only internals changed). Keep the graph acyclic.

Sharing configuration: the old `subprojects { }` / `allprojects { }` blocks in the root script are discouraged because they cross project boundaries and break with isolated projects and the configuration cache. The recommended way is a **convention plugin**: a small precompiled script plugin in `buildSrc/src/main/kotlin/acme.java-conventions.gradle.kts` (or an included build under `build-logic/`) that applies `java`, sets the toolchain, test settings and common dependencies. Each subproject then just writes `plugins { id("acme.java-conventions") }`.

A `gradle.properties` at the root holds shared properties such as `version` and JVM settings. `./gradlew projects` prints the project tree. Composite builds (`includeBuild("../lib")`) let you substitute a published dependency with a local source checkout.
takeaways: include(...) in settings defines subprojects, addressed as :name
implementation(project(":core")) depends on a sibling
Share setup with convention plugins in buildSrc or build-logic, not subprojects { }
./gradlew :api:test runs a task in one project
pitfalls: Configuring subprojects from the root with subprojects { }, which breaks modern features like the configuration cache.

quiz.q: What is the recommended way to apply the same JDK toolchain and test setup to ten subprojects?
options: Copy the blocks into each build.gradle.kts
A shell script that edits the files
A convention plugin in buildSrc or build-logic applied by each subproject
quiz.explain: Convention plugins keep shared configuration in one place without cross-project configuration.

concepts.name: Incremental builds and the build cache
concepts.summary: Understand up-to-date checks, task inputs/outputs, the local and remote build cache, and the configuration cache.
concepts.why: Build speed depends on Gradle being able to skip work; misdeclared inputs make builds slow or wrong.
concepts.body:
Gradle avoids work at three levels.

**Up-to-date checks**: every task declares **inputs** (files, properties) and **outputs**. Before running a task, Gradle hashes the inputs; if they and the outputs match the previous run, the task is skipped with `UP-TO-DATE`. Custom tasks must declare them with `@InputFile`, `@InputDirectory`, `@Input`, `@OutputDirectory` on typed task classes, or with `inputs.files(...)` / `outputs.dir(...)` in scripts. Undeclared inputs cause stale results; undeclared outputs cause needless reruns.

**Build cache** (`org.gradle.caching=true` in `gradle.properties`): task outputs are stored keyed by the input hash, so a task whose inputs were seen before, even on another branch or **another machine** via a remote cache (Develocity, HTTP cache), is restored as `FROM-CACHE` instead of executed. Compilation and tests are cacheable; tasks must be deterministic and declare all inputs. Mark custom task types `@CacheableTask` with path sensitivity annotations.

**Configuration cache** (`org.gradle.configuration-cache=true`): serializes the result of the configuration phase so later builds skip running scripts entirely. It requires scripts and plugins to avoid `Project` access at execution time and to use providers and `Property` types.

Inspect decisions with `--info` (reasons a task ran), `--scan` for a build scan, and `./gradlew help --task x`. `--rerun-tasks` ignores up-to-date checks for debugging.
takeaways: Tasks skip when declared inputs and outputs are unchanged
The build cache restores outputs by input hash, locally or remotely
The configuration cache skips the configuration phase
Undeclared inputs cause stale builds; declare everything
pitfalls: Reading a file or environment variable in a task without declaring it as an input, so changes are never picked up.

quiz.q: What does FROM-CACHE next to a task mean?
options: The task ran faster than usual
Its inputs were cached in memory
Its outputs were restored from the build cache without executing it
The task was skipped because it has no outputs
quiz.explain: A matching input hash was found in the build cache, so the stored outputs were reused.

concepts.name: Resolution, conflicts and BOMs
concepts.summary: Control transitive versions with platforms, strict versions, exclusions, substitutions and dependency locking.
concepts.why: Diamond conflicts and vulnerable transitives are everyday problems; Gradle gives precise tools to fix them.
concepts.body:
When the dependency graph is resolved, each module ends up with exactly one version per configuration. Gradle picks the **highest requested version** by default; this differs from Maven's nearest-wins rule. `./gradlew dependencyInsight --dependency <name> --configuration runtimeClasspath` shows every path and why a version won.

Tools to shape the result:

- **Platforms / BOMs**: `implementation(platform("org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-dependencies:3.4.4"))` imports a Maven BOM so all its modules get aligned versions. `enforcedPlatform` overrides even higher requests.
- **Rich versions**: `implementation("com.foo:bar") { version { strictly("[1.2, 2.0[") ; prefer("1.4") } }`.
- **Constraints** adjust transitive versions without adding a direct dependency (e.g. to fix a CVE).
- **Exclusions**: `implementation("x:y:1.0") { exclude(group = "commons-logging") }` drops an unwanted transitive.
- **Substitution** in `configurations.all { resolutionStrategy.dependencySubstitution { ... } }` replaces a module with another or with a project.
- `resolutionStrategy.failOnVersionConflict()` makes conflicts explicit.
- **Capabilities** detect mutually exclusive libraries (e.g. two logging bindings).

**Dependency locking** (`dependencyLocking { lockAllConfigurations() }` and `./gradlew dependencies --write-locks`) records resolved versions in `gradle.lockfile`, so builds stay reproducible even with ranges. **Dependency verification** checks checksums and signatures of downloaded artifacts.

Separate configurations (`compileClasspath`, `runtimeClasspath`, `testRuntimeClasspath`) may resolve to different versions, which is expected.
takeaways: Gradle resolves conflicts to the highest version unless told otherwise
platform(BOM) aligns versions across a family of modules
Constraints, strict versions and exclusions adjust transitives
Locking and verification make resolution reproducible and safe

quiz.q: Two transitive paths request library X at 1.2 and 1.5. Which does Gradle pick by default?
options: The one closest to the root, like Maven
quiz.explain: Gradle's default conflict resolution selects the highest requested version.

concepts.name: Publishing artifacts
concepts.summary: Publish libraries to Maven repositories with maven-publish, including POM metadata, sources and signing.
concepts.why: Sharing a library with other teams or the world means producing a correct Maven publication.
takeaways: maven-publish creates publications from the java component
api maps to Maven compile scope, implementation to runtime
withSourcesJar/withJavadocJar, POM metadata and signing are needed for Central
Keep credentials in properties or environment variables

quiz.q: A consumer builds with Maven. How does your Gradle implementation dependency appear in the published POM?
quiz.explain: implementation dependencies are needed at run time but not for compiling against your API, so they map to runtime scope.

concepts.name: Writing plugins and lazy configuration
concepts.summary: Build reusable binary plugins with extensions, Property and Provider types, and typed tasks that follow Gradle's lazy APIs.
concepts.why: Convention and tooling plugins are how large organizations standardize builds; the lazy API is what makes them cache-friendly.
concepts.body:
A **binary plugin** is a class implementing `Plugin<Project>`, usually written in Kotlin in `build-logic` (an included build) or a standalone repository published to a plugin repository. Its `apply(project)` method registers tasks, applies other plugins and creates an **extension** that users configure.

Gradle's modern API is **lazy**:

- Use `Property<T>`, `ListProperty<T>`, `RegularFileProperty` and `DirectoryProperty` for extension and task fields, with `abstract val` so Gradle injects managed instances.
- Wire values with providers instead of reading them eagerly: `task.outputDir.set(ext.outputDir)` links the two; the value is computed only when the task runs. Transform with `map { }` and `flatMap { }`; `project.provider { }` wraps arbitrary code.
- Register tasks with `tasks.register`, configure others with `tasks.named`, and avoid `project.afterEvaluate`.
- Never call `project` or `Project` services from `@TaskAction`; inject services (`ExecOperations`, `FileSystemOperations`, `ObjectFactory`) via `@Inject` instead. This keeps tasks compatible with the configuration cache.

Annotate task properties (`@Input`, `@InputFiles`, `@OutputDirectory`, `@Internal`, `@Nested`) so up-to-date checks and caching work; mark the task `@CacheableTask` when outputs are deterministic. Work can be parallelized with the **Worker API**.

Test plugins with **Gradle TestKit** (`GradleRunner`), which runs a real build in a temp directory, and declare plugin ids in the `gradlePlugin { plugins { } }` block of the `java-gradle-plugin` so they can be applied by id. Publish with the `com.gradle.plugin-publish` plugin.
takeaways: A plugin class registers tasks and creates an extension in apply()
Use Property/Provider types and map/flatMap for lazy wiring
Annotate task inputs/outputs; inject services instead of using Project in actions
Test with TestKit's GradleRunner
pitfalls: Reading extension values eagerly in apply(), before the user's build script has set them.

quiz.q: Why wire task.message.set(ext.message) instead of task.message.set(ext.message.get()) inside apply()?
options: At apply time the user hasn't configured the extension yet; the provider link defers reading until execution
quiz.explain: Plugins are applied before the configuring block runs, so eager get() would read the default or fail; providers resolve lazily.

concepts.name: Build performance tuning
concepts.summary: Profile builds with scans and --profile, tune daemon memory, parallelism, configuration cache and remote caching.
concepts.why: Slow builds cost teams hours a day; most slowness has a diagnosable cause.
concepts.body:
Measure first. `./gradlew build --scan` publishes a **build scan** (Develocity) with a timeline of tasks, configuration time, cache hits and dependency downloads; `--profile` writes a local HTML report to `build/reports/profile`. Look for: long configuration phase, tasks that are never up-to-date, tests dominating, and serial execution.

Settings in `gradle.properties` (project or `~/.gradle`):

- `org.gradle.parallel=true` runs independent subprojects' tasks concurrently; `org.gradle.workers.max` caps workers.
- `org.gradle.caching=true` enables the build cache; add a remote cache so CI and developers share outputs.
- `org.gradle.configuration-cache=true` eliminates configuration time on repeated builds.
- `org.gradle.jvmargs=-Xmx4g -XX:+UseParallelGC` sizes the daemon; too little memory shows as long GC pauses, too much starves compilers and test JVMs.
- `org.gradle.vfs.watch=true` (default) keeps file system state between builds.

Structural fixes often matter more: split large modules so compile avoidance and caching bite, keep configuration-phase code cheap (no file I/O or network), use `tasks.register` not `tasks.create`, prefer `implementation` over `api` to limit recompilation cascades, and run slow integration tests in their own task.

For tests, `maxParallelForks`, `forkEvery` and JUnit 5's parallel execution help. Keep the daemon alive in CI (or use `--no-daemon` with a persistent cache); cold JVMs and dependency downloads dominate CI time, so cache `~/.gradle/caches` and `~/.gradle/wrapper`.

Upgrading Gradle, the JDK and plugins regularly brings free performance work.
takeaways: Measure with --scan or --profile before changing anything
parallel, caching and configuration cache are the big three switches
Size the daemon JVM sensibly and cache ~/.gradle in CI
Modularize and keep configuration cheap for structural wins
pitfalls: Giving the daemon a huge heap and wondering why test JVMs and the OS are swapping.

quiz.q: A build scan shows every compileJava task running on every build despite no code changes. What's the likely cause?
options: A task input that changes each build (timestamp, undeclared file) invalidates up-to-date checks
quiz.explain: Volatile or undeclared inputs defeat incremental builds, so tasks always rerun.

concepts.name: Variants, attributes and capabilities
concepts.summary: Understand variant-aware resolution: how attributes pick jars vs classes, JVM versions and feature variants, and how to debug it.
concepts.why: Cryptic 'no matching variant' errors and multi-flavor Android or multiplatform libraries all come down to this model.
concepts.body:
Gradle dependencies are not just coordinates: each resolved module exposes several **variants** (for a Java library: `apiElements`, `runtimeElements`, `sourcesElements`, `javadocElements`), and a consuming configuration selects one by matching **attributes**.

Standard attributes include `org.gradle.usage` (`java-api` vs `java-runtime`), `org.gradle.category` (`library`, `platform`, `documentation`), `org.gradle.libraryelements` (`jar`, `classes`, `resources`), `org.gradle.jvm.version` (the target JVM) and, for Kotlin Multiplatform and Android, platform and build-type attributes. `compileClasspath` asks for `java-api` + `classes` when possible, which is why compilation can consume class directories of sibling projects without building jars.

The rules are published in Gradle Module Metadata (`.module` files) next to POMs, so variant selection also works for published libraries. A Maven POM is mapped to two synthetic variants.

Common errors and fixes:

- "No matching variant" usually means the producer targets a newer JVM (`org.gradle.jvm.version=21`) than the consumer's toolchain, or an Android/KMP library lacks a variant for your platform. Align toolchains or add the missing target.
- Ambiguity errors appear when two variants match equally; add a disambiguation rule or request a more specific attribute.

**Capabilities** declare what a variant provides; two modules providing the same capability conflict (`slf4j-simple` vs `logback-classic` style bindings). **Feature variants** (`java { registerFeature("mongo") { usingSourceSet(...) } }`) publish optional features with their own dependencies, consumed with `requireCapabilities`.

Debug with `./gradlew outgoingVariants` (what a project offers) and `./gradlew resolvableConfigurations` (what it asks for), and `dependencyInsight`, which prints the selected variant and attributes.
takeaways: Modules expose variants; configurations select one by matching attributes
usage, category, libraryelements and jvm.version are the key attributes
'No matching variant' is usually a JVM target or platform mismatch
outgoingVariants and resolvableConfigurations show both sides

quiz.q: Your library compiled with a JDK 21 toolchain is consumed by a project on JDK 17. What happens?
options: It works; Gradle downgrades the bytecode
Resolution fails: no variant matches org.gradle.jvm.version 17 (or lower)
Gradle silently uses the runtime variant
quiz.explain: The producer's variants carry jvm.version=21, which a JDK 17 consumer cannot accept, so variant matching fails.
